newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British manufacturing output slumps in May.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British manufacturing output slumps in May.

text.p: Output in the British manufacturing industry slumped in May, hit badly by the strong pound, but analysts said on Monday that the independent Bank of England was still likely to raise interest rates this week.

Figures on Monday registered the biggest monthly fall in manufacturing output for nearly four years as sterling, which has leapt 21 percent on a trade-weighted basis since August last year, punished exporters.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said manufacturing output fell 1.1 percent in May compared with April, pushing the year-on-year growth rate down to 1.0 percent from 2.7 percent in the year to April.

The wider measure of industrial production, which includes output from the water and power utilities as well as manufacturers, fared little better. It fell 0.9 percent in May and by 0.2 percent in the year to May.
Economists, who had expected a small rise in manufacturing output, said the fall was a worry for the Bank of England.
But it was not likely to stop the central bank raising interest rates at a meeting this week due to a consumer economy which is booming in sharp contrast to the manufacturing sector.
"The primary concern of the bank's monetary policy committee will be the strength of demand rather than the weakness of manufacturing output," said John O'Sullivan, UK economist at NatWest Markets.
"It remains likely that the manufacturing sector will be sacrificed on the altar of consumer buoyancy."

The monetary policy committee's decision on rates will be made public at midday on Thursday. It raised rates by a quarter point to 6.5 percent in June and is widely expected to raise them again this week.
A poll conducted by Reuters after last week's budget found that 21 out of 24 economists forecast rates would rise on Thursday, with a clear majority expecting a quarter point increase.

Last week's budget raised the overall tax burden by almost six billion pounds ($10 billion). But most economists think the measures will fail to dampen consumer spending since the tax rises were largely directed at the corporate sector.

However, the weak output figures complicate the economic picture. If interest rates rise on Thursday, it could propel the pound to even greater heights, further damaging the export-sensitive manufacturing sector.

The ONS said there was no indication in May that the pound -- which has also gained around 30 percent against the mark since August -- was affecting manufacturing output and export levels had held up well.
"Although the ONS said there is no obvious sign that sterling strength is having an effect on output, there will be suspicion to the contrary," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.

Britain's trade gap was likely to deteriorate later this year as export growth was squeezed by the pound. "It will be of little comfort to exporters now but a growing trade gap will ultimately put downward pressure on the pound."
The pound dropped almost two pfennigs to 2.9320 marks after the output figures but recovered slightly in midday trade to stand at 2.9379/88 marks.
